edges.description: Structurally abnormal extracellular collagen matrix impairs matrix-dependent latent TGF-beta sequestration and stimulates high-turnover remodeling.
Compromised tensile strength and mineralization of the type I collagen matrix directly cause bone fragility and recurrent fractures.
Impaired intramembranous ossification of the calvarial collagen matrix produces accessory sutural Wormian bones.
Weakened trabecular bone matrix in vertebral bodies leads to compression fractures under axial load.
Disorganized collagen fibrils and impaired mineralization reduce areal and volumetric bone mineral density.
High-turnover bone remodeling and growth plate matrix disorganization diminish childhood longitudinal growth velocity.
High-turnover cortical osteopenia and microfractures under weight-bearing loads cause long-bone bowing.
Asymmetric vertebral remodeling and compression fractures drive progressive thoracolumbar scoliosis.
Skeletal fragility and lower-limb bowing delay standing and ambulation milestones after sitting is achieved.
Remodeling of softened basicranial bone under cranial load permits upward protrusion of the odontoid process into the foramen magnum.
Mechanical loading across osteopenic, actively remodeling femoral shafts produces anterolateral femoral bowing.
High-turnover bone resorption, microfractures, and skeletal deformity cause chronic bone pain.

evidence.reference_title: Incorporating the patient perspective in the study of rare bone disease: insights from the osteogenesis imperfecta community.
evidence.snippet: Participants noted that while fractures and brittle bones are the most common feature of OI, a number of body systems are under-studied in this disorder. They particularly emphasized breathing, hearing, and the effects of aging as primary concerns that researchers and physicians may not fully understand or address. Other areas included pain, gastrointestinal problems, mental health, nutrition, menopause/pregnancy, and basilar invagination.

nodes.description: Long-bone bowing can occur in type IV OI, particularly in the femur.

evidence.reference_title: Management of Combined Fracture Neck of Femur and Femoral Deformity in Osteogenesis Imperfecta Patient: A Case Report.
evidence.snippet: The bone fragility and repeated fractures produce deformities of the long bones especially in femur and tibia. However, neck of femur (NOF) fractures in OI are rarely described. A 11-year-old male patient known to have OI (Sillence type IV) sustained a NOF fracture after a fall. He also had proximal femoral anterolateral bowing proximally and over an intramedullary (IM) rod inserted 4 years back.

evidence.reference_title: Excessive transforming growth factor-β signaling is a common mechanism in osteogenesis imperfecta.
evidence.snippet: Here, we show that excessive transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) signaling is a mechanism of OI in both recessive (Crtap(-/-)) and dominant (Col1a2(tm1.1Mcbr)) OI mouse models. In the skeleton, we find higher expression of TGF-β target genes, higher ratio of phosphorylated Smad2 to total Smad2 protein and higher in vivo Smad2 reporter activity.

evidence.reference_title: Collagen transport and related pathways in Osteogenesis Imperfecta
evidence.snippet: The production of collagen entails a complex process, starting from the production of the collagen Iα1 and collagen Iα2 chains in the endoplasmic reticulum, during and after which procollagen is subjected to a plethora of posttranslational modifications by chaperones. After reaching the Golgi organelle, procollagen is destined to the extracellular matrix where it forms collagen fibrils.

evidence.reference_title: How common is hearing impairment in osteogenesis imperfecta?
evidence.snippet: It was found that the most common age of onset was in the second, third and fourth decades of life. At the age of 50 approximately 50 per cent of the patients had symptoms of hearing impairment; over the next 20 years there was little further increase. Differences were shown between patients with different clinical types of osteogenesis imperfecta as delineated in the Sillence classification; hearing loss was significantly less common in the type IV disease than in the type I disorder.

evidence.reference_title: Osteogenesis imperfecta with dominant inheritance and normal sclerae.
evidence.snippet: This paper reports the clinical and radiographical features of 48 patients from 16 families with Type 4 osteogenesis imperfecta and compares the findings with those of the classical disorder with blue sclerae (Type 1 osteogenesis imperfecta). The two types are similar in usually causing a mild disease but with a wide range of severity, and in both types the rate of fracture declines in adolescence.
